about: Traiectum (Utrecht), one port. Written 6 Oct 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/traiectum.md and the spine (Design/content/spine.json). A draft in the game's own files, for the user to overwrite. (?) marks what could not be checked.

ports.summary: A Roman stone fort on the south bank of the Rhine, given to Willibrord's church: two small churches, a school, a bishop's household and a bank where boats are drawn up. In 793 there is no market, no toll and no mint here: the church buys wax, wine, oil, incense and books, and pays in silver, in letters and in its good word. A merchant comes for the bishop's custom, for the road north by the Vecht to the Almere, and because the men who can read live here.
ports.seasons: The year runs by the church: fish and fasting through Lent, the river high with meltwater at Easter, letters and ships moving from Pentecost. Saint Willibrord's day and Martinmas close it with goose and the new wine from up the Rhine, then forty days of fast to Christmas while the boats lie on the bank.

history.text: About this year King Dagobert has a chapel built in the old Roman fort. The Frisians pull it down.
Willibrord is made archbishop of the Frisians. Pippin gives him the fort, which the people there call Wiltaburg and the Franks Traiectum. He builds Saint Salvator's and raises Saint Martin's again.
Charles Martel gives the fort and its land, with Vechten up the river, to the church of Utrecht.
Willibrord dies on 7 November. He is buried at Echternach, not here.
About this year Saint Martin's becomes the bishop's church, and Gregory, never a bishop, rules the house and its school as abbot until about 775.
The body of Boniface, killed at Doccinga, comes by boat over the Aelmere. The count reads King Pippin's ban on moving it. The church bell rings with no hand on it, and the body goes on to Mainz.
Liudger, schooled here and then at York under Alcuin, comes home with books when the Angles and the Frisians fall out at York.
The king gives the church Leusden, four woods in Eemland and the Upkirika at Dorestad.

About this year Alcuin sends a poem down the Rhine. It greets Bishop Alberic as 'vaccipotens praesul', mighty in cows, and Prior Hadda, who will serve honey, porridge and butter, for Frisia yields no oil or wine.
history.source: Alcuin, carmen 4 (MGH Poetae I, 220-3), paraphrased; written by 782

history.text: About this year Hamacar is bishop. Nothing but his name and his years is known.
Ricfried is bishop after Hamacar, until 815 or 816.
This year a Danish fleet came by Utrecht to Dorestad and plundered it.
Between 835 and 838 Bishop Frederik is stabbed by two men after Mass. Later writers blame the Empress Judith, or men of Walcheren.
history.source: nl.wikipedia 'Frederik van Utrecht' (the year is not sure)

history.text: Rorik the Dane takes Dorestad and is granted it. One account gives him Utrecht too.
While Rorik is away in Denmark other Danes sack Utrecht. The churches are destroyed and Bishop Hunger flees.
history.source: nl.wikipedia 'Hunger van Utrecht', 'Dom van Utrecht'; Annales Fuldenses 857 (?)

history.text: King Lothar II gives the clergy of Utrecht Saint Peter's at Sint-Odilienberg to live in. Later the bishops sit at Deventer.
Northmen take Utrecht and Nijmegen and winter there.
About this year Bishop Balderik brings the see home. He rebuilds the churches, the school and the walls, with gates, bastions and a bridge on the west side.
history.source: nl.wikipedia 'Balderik van Utrecht'; De Bruijn, 'De burcht Trecht'

history.text: King Otto gives the bishop the mint, and Muiden with its toll on the Vecht. (One source puts the mint in 936.)
The Northmen come, a year after they burned Tiel. The merchants set fire to their own harbour quarter and go into the fort. No attack follows.
history.source: Alpertus of Metz, De diversitate temporum I.8-10: 'portum omnem ipsi incenderunt' (chronicle_793.json has it under 1006)

history.text: Bishop Ansfried, once the emperor's sword-bearer and blind for five years, dies on 3 May. Utrecht men carry off his body while the people of the Heiligenberg fight a fire that did not start by chance.
Fire takes the cathedral and the bishop's house.
Bishop Adelbold is with the emperor's army that Count Dirk beats at Vlaardingen.
Adelbold's new cathedral is consecrated before the Emperor Henry and twelve bishops.
history.source: nl.wikipedia 'Dom van Utrecht' (26 June or 26 July: the sources differ)

history.text: The Emperor Conrad dies here at Pentecost, 4 June. His body goes up the Rhine to Speyer; his entrails stay in the cathedral.
King Henry III gives Groningen to Saint Martin's. About now the emperor's palace of Lofen stands in the fort, of tuff, with a row of sandstone columns.
Bishop Bernold dies on 19 July and is buried in Saint Peter's, one of the three churches he built.
The king gives Bishop Willem the county of West Frisia, on parchment.

eras.text: A church stronghold and nothing else. Patched Roman walls, two small stone churches, a timber school, the bishop's hall, and a sloping bank west of the fort where a dozen boats lie. The trade passes by to Dorestad; the church buys what an altar and a scriptorium eat.

The same place with its ears up. The fleet of 834 went by on its way to Dorestad and comes back most summers. The bishop keeps a boat ready, the school buries its ink horns, and after 850 the toll down the river is taken in Rorik's name.

Wasted. The churches are roofless, the bishop lives at Deventer, and yellow flood clay lies over the strand where the houses stood. A few boatmen and fishers keep the crossing. A priest comes from inland to say Mass on Martin's day.

Balderik is home. Scaffolds stand on the walls, there are new gates and a bridge on the west side, the school has boys again and a king's son among them. Merchants who lost Dorestad build on the strand, which they now call the Stathe.

A bishop's town with a mint and a toll. Timber houses and revetments run along the Vecht side; grain, wine, stone, glass and pots come in, herring goes out, and goods that pass must be offered for sale here.

The merchants burned their own quarter when the Northmen came and have built it again, closer under the wall. The cathedral burns in 1017 and stands new in 1023. The bishop is a count now and rides with the emperor's army.

Stone everywhere. Bernold raises Saint Peter's, Saint John's and Saint Paul's around the cathedral, the emperor has a palace in the fort, and an emperor dies in it. The merchants have a church of their own on the Stathe and long barges on the Vecht.

sites.name: The strand under the wall
sites.see: In front, a sloping bank of trodden clay with a dozen boats drawn up on rollers and a tow-rope drying over a rail. Behind, the pale tuff wall of the fort with two low church roofs showing over it. Smoke from eel fires, wet hemp, and a bell counting the hours of prayer.
sites.source: De Bruijn, 'De vicus Stathe': Carolingian pottery of 750-1000 on the strand, flood clay and no houses from about 850 to after 900; no jetty: boats drawn up the bank (dossier 1)

sites.name: The crossing at the Vecht mouth
sites.see: The river bends round the north of the fort and splits: the Vecht goes north through reeds toward the Almere, the old Rhine west toward the sea. In front a flat ferry on a pole and a half-hollowed oak on trestles, chips all round it. Behind, the dark line of the peat bog. Adze strokes, curlews, tar.
sites.source: Traiectum means a crossing (nl.wikipedia 'Utrecht (stad)'); the widened logboat built here: Vleuten 1, felled after about 734 (Design/content/ships.md). Where the Vecht left the Rhine is not sure (?)

sites.name: Hildeburg's ale-house
sites.see: A low reed-roofed house on the levee above the strand, its door open to the river. In front a bench, a tub of ale under a wet cloth and eels hanging split in the smoke. Behind, the wall of the fort gone gold in the evening. Boatmen talk Frisian; a clerk from the school pretends he is not there.
sites.source: invented; boatmen, fishers and levee farmers lived below the fort (Research/traiectum_c800_notes.md)

sites.name: The gate of the fort
sites.see: A Roman gateway of grey tuff with newer, rougher stone let into it and an oak door hung where an arch once was. In front, a porter's bench and a begging bowl. Through the gate a yard of trodden earth and the west end of Saint Martin's. Cold in the shadow even at midsummer.
sites.source: De Bruijn, 'De burcht Trecht': a fort of 126 by 152 m, tuff walls of about AD 210 patched in the 7th century, gates north, east and south found by digging

sites.name: Saint Martin's
sites.see: A small stone church, the bishop's own, with a wooden bell frame beside the door. Inside, one lamp before the altar, wax candles on feast days only, a painted cloth on the east wall. Behind it the roof of Saint Salvator's, a stone's throw away. Incense when there is any; damp stone always.
sites.source: nl.wikipedia 'Dom van Utrecht': Dagobert's chapel of about 630, rebuilt by Willibrord, the cathedral from about 750, destroyed 857, rebuilt after about 920, burned 1017. The bell: Willibald's Life of Boniface, 754

sites.name: Saint Salvator's, the old minster
sites.see: Willibrord's church: a plain hall of tuff eighteen paces long with a smaller room on its east end, where the dead of the house lie in limestone coffins under the floor. In front the clergy file in two by two. Morning light through three small windows. Psalms, sung slowly.
sites.source: nl.wikipedia 'Sint-Salvatorkerk (Utrecht)': a hall of 12 by 18 m with an east annex of 9 by 12 m where limestone sarcophagi were found; Bishops Ricfried, Frederik and Odilbald lie here; Odulf's relics brought here by Balderik

sites.name: The school house
sites.see: A long timber house against the inner face of the wall. In front, boys on benches with wax tablets on their knees; a master walking behind them with a switch he does not use. Behind, an iron-bound chest under the one glazed window, and a sloped desk with a book open on it. Tallow, ink of oak gall, chalk.
sites.source: The school of Gregory, where Liudger learned 756-767 (en.wikipedia 'Ludger'); timber buildings inside the walls (?) (dossier 2). The key riddle: riddles_793.json riddle_symphosius_04_clavis

sites.name: The prior's store
sites.see: A half-sunk store room of old Roman footings roofed with thatch. In front, a scale hung from a beam and a tally board; cakes of wax stacked like loaves, two casks, one jar of oil kept under lock. Behind, sacks counted and counted again. It smells of honey and of mice.
sites.source: The church buys wax, wine, oil, incense, books and Lenten fish (Design/research_trade_seasons_and_hints.md: a guess); there is no market here in 793 (dossier 4, 8): this is a buyer's store, not a market

sites.name: The guest house
sites.see: A timber hall by the gate with a hearth in the middle of the floor and straw along the walls. In front a table with a bowl of porridge, a crock of butter and a comb of honey; no wine. Behind, a monk asleep sitting up with a letter case under his arm. Wood smoke and wet wool.
sites.source: Alcuin, carmen 4: Hadda serves honey, porridge and butter, 'utpute non oleum nec vinum Fresia fundit'. Guests kept apart under one monk's care: Rule of Benedict 53

sites.name: The bishop's hall
sites.see: A timber hall on stone footings beside Saint Martin's. In front, a high seat with a carved back, a deacon at a writing desk and a chest of charters with three locks. Behind, a hanging of red wool gone brown. Light from the door only. The talk is low and in two tongues.
sites.source: The fort is the bishop's by the gift of 723; the see's charters (Oorkondenboek van het Sticht Utrecht). The bishop's house burned with the cathedral in 1017 (nl.wikipedia 'Dom van Utrecht')

sites.name: The Stathe
sites.see: The old strand built over: a street of timber houses with their gables to the river and their back doors to the fort's west bridge. In front, trestles of pots, glass, cloth and salt fish; a merchants' church of wood, later of stone. Behind, Balderik's new wall. Hammering, haggling, a pig loose.
sites.source: De Bruijn, 'De vicus Stathe'; nl.wikipedia 'Stathe', 'Buurkerk': the merchants' quarter of the 10th century, their church of the 10th or early 11th; burned by its own people in 1007 (Alpertus)

sites.name: The Vecht side
sites.see: A long bank faced with oak posts and wattle, planks of old boats nailed in among them. In front, three long barges nose to tail and a hollowed oak ship with a short towing mast. Behind, storehouses with their doors to the water. Tar, herring brine, wet oak.
sites.source: The Waterstraat dig, 1974-81: 420 m of revetments, timber houses and ships of the 10th to 12th century (Research/traiectum_c800_notes.md); planks of a Norse-built keel ship reused in the quay (Design/content/ships.md, Utrecht 4). The bishop's toll: Muiden 953, moved here 975 (?)

sites.name: The bishop's mint
sites.see: A small stone room inside the gate with a barred window. In front, a moneyer at a block with a die in one fist and a hammer in the other; a boy cutting blanks with shears. Behind, a scale no bigger than a hand. The ring of the hammer carries to the Stathe.
sites.source: Otto I gives the mint to the bishop in 953 (nl.wikipedia 'Balderik van Utrecht'), or 936 (nl.wikipedia 'Stathe'). Pennies in the bishop's own name only from Bernold on (?) (numista 373398). No moneyer is named

sites.name: Adelbold's cathedral
sites.see: A great new church of tuff on the place of the old Saint Martin's, with round arches and a high west end; after 1050 three more churches stand round it. In the choir floor a stone marked for an emperor. Candles by the score, and a choir of canons.
sites.source: nl.wikipedia 'Dom van Utrecht': consecrated 1023 before Henry II and twelve bishops. Conrad II's entrails ('exta' on the choir stone) from 1039 (nl.wikipedia 'Koenraad II de Salier'). Bernold's churches: nl.wikipedia 'Pieterskerk (Utrecht)', 'Janskerk (Utrecht)', 'Paulusabdij (Utrecht)'

people.name: Hamacar
people.trait: Keeper of Willibrord's house and its school: careful, formal, more a steward of lands than a preacher.
people.want: Wax, wine and oil for Saint Martin's; a ship that will carry letters to York and bring books back.
people.fear: The East Frisian rising reaching the Vecht; the count taking the church's fines.
people.voice: Formal and unhurried; speaks of the blessed Willibrord as of a neighbour who has stepped out.
people.looks: About fifty, tonsured, a white linen alb under a dark wool cloak, a bishop's ring and a plain staff with a curled head, a deacon with a book beside him.
knows: what the church will pay for wax, wine, oil and incense
what the king has ordered about grain and prices
who carries letters to York and who has failed to
the church's lands and its tenth at Dorestad

ties.note: the same person
Liudger was schooled in his church and sends to him for priests
bishop and count dispute every fine
writes to him for books; has not met him
his prior, who was here before him and will say so
the count's steward counts the church's tenth at Dorestad too closely
the toll man counts the church's tenth of the tenth as if it were his own teeth
his priest at the upper church of Dorestad: overworked, obedient, and always asking for a bell
the master of his school: a better scholar than the bishop, as both of them know
a priest of Echternach's church, on a marsh where Saint Martin also claims the tithe
the clerk copies for him what the king's chest holds touching Saint Martin's lands
sends him chrism and advice, and has never settled whose diocese the hill lies in (?)
writes each Easter for books and a bell, and gets a blessing
brings the bishop's tenth of the toll to Traiectum himself each Martinmas, counted twice
his priest on the edge of the baptised world, sent north with one book
his priest at the martyr's church, who sends the tithe south by any boat
a young priest of his school, lost sight of in the rising
a brother bishop up the river; they exchange wax for wine and complaints for complaints
a tenant of Saint Martin's at Doccinga with a story of the martyr's day, which his clerks are to hear before she dies
the priest on the Scheldt sends to his school for a book to copy from, and for boys who can read it
from 794 or 795 the archbishop at Cologne is over him, and the orders come down by river
the king's steward at Cologne promised him a cargo for the poor before harvest; the grain exists and the boat does not
does not know he has an enemy on the island: his house keeps the story of the idol, and the man's forefather is the villain of it

lines.greet: You are the one with the small boat. Sit. The blessed Willibrord also came in a small boat.
lines.greet_again: You came back when you said you would. That is rarer on this river than wine.
rumour: East of the Lauwers they have burned the churches again. Liudger is driven out. I have asked where he is and nobody can tell me.
The king has set a price on bread and told his bishops to feed the hungry. He did not send the grain.
The count's steward at Dorestat has measured our tenth three times this year. It comes out smaller each time.
lines.trade: Wax first. Then wine for the altar, and oil. Sell them to my prior at a fair weight and I will remember who did.
lines.warm: A house that carries my letters does not stand alone on its reckoning day. Tell the steward I said so.
lines.saying: The blessed Willibrord says nothing about the price of wax. I take that for trust.
lines.farewell: Go with God, and keep my letters above the bilge.

people.source: nl.wikipedia 'Lijst van bisschoppen van Utrecht': Hamacarus, about 790-806. The man is real; nothing else is known of him, and his character, his age and his words are invented (spine.json cast.hamacar)

people.name: Hadda
people.trait: The old prior: keeps the gate, the store and the guest table himself, and has outlasted four masters of the house.
people.want: The store full before Lent, and one guest in his life who praises the porridge.
people.fear: A weight he did not check; dying before somebody learns where everything is kept.
people.voice: Dry, slow, counts as he talks; never says a price first.
people.looks: Near sixty, short and broad, a grey fringe round the tonsure, a brown habit with a rope of keys, a wooden spoon stuck in his belt.
knows: what the store lacks and what it will give for it
every guest who has slept here since Gregory's day
the poem a York master once wrote about his table
which Dorestad merchants give a fair weight

ties.note: his fourth master; he compares them aloud
fed him once, and was put in a poem for it
they were boys together under Gregory
the black-haired merchant who gave a poet no lodging, and gives the church short wax
the widow sends alms by other hands; he knows whose they are
her ale draws his boatmen and his schoolboys
the ferryman pays the bank's rent in ferrying, and the prior keeps the tally in his head
the toll man from the Almere brings the saint's tenth himself each Martinmas, and swears at the Vecht the whole length of the guest table

lines.greet: Honey, porridge and butter. Frisia gives no oil and no wine, as a better man than you has already said.
lines.greet_again: You again. I kept your place by the fire. The straw is the same straw.
rumour: A monk of York slept here two nights and would not put his satchel down even to eat. He is asking for a ship.
Hrotberct at Dorestat has wax, and a thumb on the scale. Go to him last.
The boys say the master has a riddle he gives only to strangers. I have the answer on my belt.
lines.trade: Put it on my scale, not yours. Wax by the cake, wine by the cask, and we shall both sleep.
lines.warm: I told the bishop you weigh fair. He wrote nothing down, which with him is a good sign.
lines.saying: A bishop mighty in cows needs no vineyard. That is what we tell the guests.
lines.farewell: Come before Lent next time. After it I have nothing to sell you and nothing to buy.

people.source: Alcuin, carmen 4 (MGH Poetae I, 220-3): Hadda, prior about 780, serves honey, porridge and butter. That he is alive in 793, his people, his age and his character are not known (?)

people.name: Radger
people.trait: Master of the cathedral school: learned beside Liudger under Gregory and stayed behind when Liudger went to York.
people.want: Books the chest does not hold; calfskin and ink; one pupil who will go further than he did.
people.fear: Damp, moths and fire, in that order; that the York books will be asked back.
people.voice: Asks questions he knows the answer to, then waits; Frisian with Latin dropped in like salt.
people.looks: About fifty, thin, stooped, ink on the right thumb, a black habit patched at the elbows, a small iron key on a thong round his neck.
knows: what a book is worth and to whom
the books Liudger carried home from York, and the year
Latin riddles, and which merchants can be taught letters
who at York will receive a Frisian and who will not

ties.note: they shared a bench under Gregory; Liudger went to York and he did not
the York monk brings him news of books and takes away his copies
has never met him and measures himself against him daily
boys together; the prior keeps him in tallow
the bishop is the school's lord
will hear the boy his letters when the boat lies here, if the boy is aboard
his pupil, now a priest on the Ems; he pays for any news of him
sent north to the Almere shore with one book, which he asks after
she sends his truant boys back by the ear, and keeps their pennies
the palace clerk sends him riddles by passing boats; he sends back the answers, and a harder one
the priest on the Scheldt writes when a boat goes; he answers one letter in three
the scribe at Ganda: they lend each other exemplars by boat, and argue by the same boat
they trade copies up and down the river, and each thinks the other got the better book

lines.greet: Sit there, merchant. Here is one for you. What opens a shut house and shuts an open one, and is kept by the man it keeps?
lines.greet_again: You are back, and dry. Is the thing I gave you still in your head, or did the sea have it?
rumour: The chest holds the books Liudger carried from York. He came home the year the Angles and our people fell out there.
York had more books than all Frisia has cows. I am told so by men who have seen both.
A merchant's son I taught now reads at Dorestat for silver. He has a riddle about iron teeth; ask him.
lines.trade: Calfskin, scraped thin. Gall ink. Red, if you ever see red. I pay in copies, which keep better than pennies.
lines.warm: Sit down. I will show you what a book is worth, so the next man who sells you one cannot.
lines.saying: The chest is full of holy words and knows none of them. I have had pupils like that.
lines.farewell: Keep it dry. Everything I say to anyone ends with that.

people.source: invented; the school is Gregory's, where Liudger learned 756-767 (en.wikipedia 'Ludger'). The riddle is Symphosius 4, the key (texts_793.json symphosius_04_clavis); the chest saying turns Aldhelm's riddle 89 (texts_793.json aldhelm_89_arca_libraria)

people.name: Aldlef
people.trait: Keeps the crossing and the bank, pilots the Vecht to the Almere, and hollows an oak into a boat every second winter.
people.want: Rhineland oak, long and straight; a son-in-law who can pole.
people.fear: A dry summer on the Vecht; the bishop's clerk learning how much he takes at the crossing.
people.voice: Few words, all about water; calls every stranger 'skipper', even boys.
people.looks: Late thirties, long arms, a short Frisian cloak, bare legs muddy to the knee, a pole twice his height and an adze in his belt.
knows: the Vecht's bends and shallows to Muiden and the Almere
who came down the river today and what lay in their boats
what a boat costs and how long the oak must lie
the tow path to Dorestad and who hires out haulers

ties.note: his elder sister; she keeps his reckoning and his secrets
the bank is church land and the rent is paid in ferrying
two steersmen who can stand an hour without speaking
the Maas pilot says river pilots only need to know left from right
sends word ahead by the Vecht boats who is coming and how laden

lines.greet: Skipper. Pull her up there, above the weed line. The river rises at night and tells nobody.
lines.greet_again: Skipper. Same place as before. I kept the rollers for you.
rumour: Three boats went north by the Vecht this morning, low in the water. Wine, by the way they steered.
The Vecht is thin above Zuilen this year. A laden boat should pole, not sail.
A priest came over the Almere in a fisher's boat with nothing but a book. From the Ems, he said. He did not say more.
lines.trade: A boat like mine takes one oak, one winter and two men. I can start at Martinmas if you bring the oak.
lines.warm: I told the Medemelacha toll man you were coming. He will not be gentle, but he will be quick.
lines.saying: The Rhine goes to the sea. The Vecht goes home.
lines.farewell: Keep to the outside of the bends, skipper.

people.source: invented; the crossing gives the place its name, and the widened logboat is built on this river from about 734 (Design/content/ships.md, Vleuten 1). Alcuin has a boat towed up 'prelongo remulco'

people.name: Hildeburg
people.trait: A boatman's widow who brews on the levee, smokes eels and hears everything said on the strand before the bishop does.
people.want: Barley malt at a price; her brother married; to be told the news first.
people.fear: A priest's sermon against her bench; a hungry spring.
people.voice: Quick, warm, teasing; answers a question with the price of something.
people.looks: Mid forties, strong forearms, a linen head cloth, a dark wool gown kilted up for work, a small bronze cross and beside it a knotted cord she does not explain.
knows: who is in harbour and who owes whom
the price of malt, eels and butter along the Vecht
which boatmen want hire and which should not be hired
what the school's clerks say when they have drunk

ties.note: her younger brother; she thinks him slow and would kill for him
he calls her bench a snare; he also buys her eels
had a fever cord from the wise woman of the Ems, by way of a boatman
the big Dorestad skipper sold her malt on trust and reminds her kindly
sends him his truant boys back by the ear

lines.greet: A new face and a small boat. Sit. The first cup is a penny for four and the news is free.
lines.greet_again: There you are. I said you would be back by this moon. Aldlef owes me an eel.
rumour: The holy island in the north was robbed by heathen men from the sea. The clerks talked of nothing else and drank double.
Thiadbod's big ship lay here two nights. He gave the porter a gift. He gives everybody a gift.
They say the bishop must feed the poor till harvest. The prior came to ask what my malt cost.
lines.trade: Malt. Bring me barley malt and I will pay you better than the church, and quicker.
lines.warm: Your man with the sore hand: I have put a cord on it. Do not tell the prior.
lines.saying: After Martin's goose, forty days of fish. Drink now.
lines.farewell: Mind the Vecht. And come and tell me what you saw.

people.source: invented; an ale-house on the levee is a guess. The knotted cord: Indiculus superstitionum 10 (amulets and knots), which the Utrecht mission preached against

people.name: Odulf
people.trait: A canon of Saint Salvator's from Brabant, sent by Bishop Frederik to preach at Stavoren and come home old.
people.want: The Frisians of the Almere shore kept in the faith; to die here, not on a road.
people.fear: The fleets; that what was done to Frederik was done by Christians.
people.voice: Gentle, a little deaf; says hard things as if remarking on the weather.
people.looks: In his fifties, later white-haired, lean, tonsured, a canon's dark cloak, a walking staff worn smooth and a small book in a leather bag.
knows: the road and the water to Stavoren
how Bishop Frederik died, and what is said of it
the fleet of 834 as one who saw it pass
which churches up the river will take in books and relics

ties.note: prays for the Dane's soul and does not trust his oath
Rorik's toll man listens to him, standing at the back
they agree that a merchant's ship is the church's road north
they never met: Balderik brings his bones home to Saint Salvator's a lifetime later
preached at the island's cross that they are half heathen; the salter answered him civilly, which was worse
brings the count more news than the palace does
his last bishop, to whom he left the list of skippers who promised a boat
the abbot who sends books and good advice to a priest among the Frisians
spoke for the lake hamlet when Saint Martin's forgave its tenth the year after the water

lines.greet: God keep you. You came by the river. Then you have seen what I am afraid to ask about.
lines.greet_again: You again, and alive. I say a psalm for every boat I know. Yours is the fourth.
rumour: The fleet came by under our wall and did not stop. We sang the office. I do not know what else there was to do.
Bishop Frederik was stabbed coming from Mass. Some say the empress, some say men of Walichrum. He named nobody.
A Dane takes the toll at Dorestat now and wears a cross for the day's business. Well. It is a beginning.
lines.trade: I buy nothing. But the house needs wax, and a boat it can trust when the sails come again.
lines.warm: If they come, take the chest from the school before you take anything of your own. I ask it of you.
lines.saying: The Frisians keep a fast better than a feast. I find that hopeful.
lines.farewell: Go safely. I am too old to learn a new skipper's name.

people.source: nl.wikipedia 'Odulfus': canon, sent to Stavoren by Bishop Frederik, died at Utrecht after 854 (feast 12 June); his birth year and his words are invented (?). Frederik's death: nl.wikipedia 'Frederik van Utrecht'

people.name: Balderik
people.trait: The bishop who brought the see home: a count's son who builds walls first and churches second, and schools a king's child.
people.want: Stone, lime and oak; merchants on his strand; relics for his altars.
people.fear: Another fleet before the gates are hung; the counts of Nifterlake.
people.voice: Brisk, a lord's Frankish; thanks a man by giving him more to do.
people.looks: As he comes home, in his twenties, tall and fair; in age heavy and white-bearded. A fur-edged cloak over the alb, a gold ring, a staff, lime dust on his shoes.
knows: what the works need and what he will pay for stone and oak
the king's court, and who has the king's ear
the toll at Muiden and the mint, once they are his
which families held ground on the strand before the sack

ties.note: came after Bishop Radboud, who lived and died in exile at Deventer
his successors keep the peace that he gave the Stathe's merchants
the king's son, schooled here from the age of four, later archbishop of Cologne
the Mainz merchant who sells him silk for the altar and pepper for the table
never met: he brings the old canon's bones home to Saint Salvator's a lifetime after his death
the count of the western coast, who counts Saint Martin's tithes there as his own to forgive

lines.greet: A merchant with a boat. If she can carry stone, we shall get on.
lines.greet_again: You. The last load was sound. I have another, and it is heavier.
rumour: The king's youngest son is in my school. He is four and corrects the deacon's Latin.
They are robbing the old Roman walls at Vechten for my gates. Rome owes us that much.
The king has given me the mint and the toll at Muiden. Go north by the Vecht and you will meet my man.
lines.trade: Tuff, lime, oak beams, lead for a roof. Bring those and take your pick of ground on the strand.
lines.warm: Your grandfather's people carried our chest inland. It is written down. Ground on the Stathe is yours without rent.
lines.saying: A church without a wall is a gift to the heathen.
lines.farewell: Come back laden. I count the days in cart loads.

people.source: nl.wikipedia 'Balderik van Utrecht'; en.wikipedia 'Balderic of Utrecht': bishop 918-975, brought the see home about 920, rebuilt churches, school and walls, taught Bruno, received the mint and Muiden's toll in 953, brought the relics of Agnes, Pontian and Odulf. His birth year (?) and his words are invented

people.name: Bernbod
people.trait: A merchant of the Stathe with a house on the Vecht side, a share in two barges and kin at Tiel: the first to pick up a torch in 1007.
people.want: A stone church for the merchants; the bishop's toll kept where it is and no higher.
people.fear: Sails on the Lek; Count Dirk's toll at the river mouth.
people.voice: Loud, friendly, swears by Saint Martin; tells the same story better each time.
people.looks: About forty, thick-set, red beard going grey, a long wool tunic with a silver cloak pin, a purse and a folding scale at his belt; one hand scarred by a burn after 1007.
knows: prices on the Stathe and at Tiel
the bishop's toll and who is free of it
what the Northmen did at Tiel and what was said to them here
who is building barges and who is selling one

ties.note: holds his ground by the peace Balderik gave the merchants
the blind bishop, once a count and the emperor's sword-bearer, whose word the Stathe trusts
says Deventer pennies are light and takes them anyway
has a name to curse for every fleet; this is the one he uses
his cousin from Tiel, burned out in 1006, whom he lodged that winter

lines.greet: By Saint Martin, a stranger with an honest boat. Tie up by mine. Show me what you are carrying, and I will tell you who should have told you to bring it here.
lines.greet_again: Here he is. I told them you would be back before the herring. Come and see what I have built.
rumour: They burned Tiel last summer. My cousin got out with his scale and his wife, in that order, he says.
We burned it ourselves. Every house on the water. They looked at the smoke and the wall and went away.
Count Dirk takes a toll at the river mouth that no king gave him. The bishop means to ask him about it with an army.
lines.trade: Grain, wine and stone come in; herring goes out. Whatever passes must be offered here first. That is the bishop's rule, not mine.
lines.warm: You carried buckets with us that day. Your berth is your berth. Nobody on this water will say otherwise.
lines.saying: A house can be built in a summer. A wall cannot. So we kept the wall.
lines.farewell: Go on, then. And if you see sails on the Lek, row first and count them after.

people.source: invented; the merchants below the fort in 1007 are Alpertus's ('portum omnem ipsi incenderunt'), none of them named. Goods of about 1000: nl.wikipedia 'Stathe'

people.name: Hunger
people.trait: The last bishop to sit at Traiectum before the Northmen: plain, stubborn, not made for courts, and unlucky in his years.
people.want: His tenth of the king's tenth from Dorestad, whoever takes the toll there; and one summer in which he need not count sails from the wall.
people.fear: That he will be the bishop who lost Saint Willibrord's house, and that the Dane who was set to guard the river will be away when it matters.
people.voice: Blunt and short; says what he will not do first, and then what he will.
people.looks: A man past fifty, short and thickset, said to be no beauty; a plain dark cloak, a worn silver cross, a staff he leans on in earnest.
knows: what the church of Utrecht holds on the rivers and the coast, by its goods register
what Rorik swore, and to which king
which houses up the Maas and the IJssel would take in a bishop and his clerks
how many boats lie on the strand tonight

ties.note: the Dane set to keep the river, who was in Denmark trying for a kingdom the summer the fleet came
Rorik's toll man, from whom he still claims Saint Martin's tenth of the tenth
the old canon died in his first years; the promise Odulf had from the skippers is all the plan he has
a brother bishop who has also lost a church to the Northmen and gone on
his canons call the islanders half heathen; the islanders have stopped sending to him
a tenant of Saint Martin's in Oostergo who still puts the rent by, though there is nobody to send it to

lines.greet: You are a Dorestat house. Then you pay a Dane his toll. I do not blame you for it. I only say that a tenth of that tenth is Saint Martin's, and I have not seen it.
lines.greet_again: Still afloat. Good. I count the boats on my strand every evening now, and yours is one I count twice.
rumour: The Dane has gone home to try for a kingdom. He left his oath here and took his ships. I would rather it had been the other way about.
King Lothar offers us a house far up the Maas if the worst comes. A bishop of Traiectum on a hill in the south. Saint Willibrord would have had something to say.
The old canon made every skipper he trusted promise him a boat for the chest. He is dead, and I have his list. Your house is on it, or it is not: you know which.
lines.saying: A wall keeps out a thief. For a fleet you need a king, and I have a Dane.
lines.farewell: Go with God, and come back by this strand. I may need the boat more than the cargo.

people.source: historical: Hunger, bishop of Utrecht 854-866, fled in 857 when Northmen wasted Utrecht while Rorik was in Denmark; Lothar II gave him the monastery of Berg (Sint Odiliënberg) in 858; he died at Prüm on 22 December 866 (nl.wikipedia 'Hunger (bisschop)'; Annales Bertiniani 857). Called a Frisian and described as ill-favoured by later tradition (?). His words, his dealings with Rorik's toll man and the list are invented.

stories.title: Letters for York
stories.summary: The bishop wants a ship that will carry his letters to York and bring books back, and the schoolmaster wants the books more than the bishop does. A house that does it well becomes the church's own carrier, with a bishop's word behind it on the Wōkerer's day.
stories.picture: The school chest open under the glazed window, a thin master lifting out a book in both hands, a merchant in a salt-stained cloak holding his own hands behind his back.

beats.text: A priest on the dam heads has a letter from York, thirteen days old with the news of the holy island, and a book that must go to Traiectum. Carried dry, it is the house's first word with the bishop.
Radger sets the key riddle, then opens the chest: the books Liudger carried home from York. He teaches what a book is worth, and to whom.
Hamacar hands over a sealed letter for York and a list of books in the deacon's hand. He names no fee. The prior names one afterwards.
Frisians have not been welcome at York since a Frisian killed a count's son there. The letter is the leave to land. Sigewine finds the book and will not let anyone else carry it aboard.
A following sea and a wet hold. The crew must choose what is kept dry: the book, the bread or themselves.
The book is read aloud on the first evening. Radger gives a standing order for calfskin, ink and wax tablets, and the bishop says before his deacon that this house carries his letters.
The palace clerk has letters from his old master, now abbot at Tours, and reads them to anyone. One asks who on the lower Rhine still carries books dry.

endings.how: The letter reached York and the book came back dry.
endings.text: The house is the church's carrier. Monks elsewhere have heard; the school orders by the year, and the bishop will stand surety on the Wōkerer's day.
endings.reward: flags bk_carried and bk_parchment; the unlocks traiectum.standing_order and traiectum.surety; standing with the Franks' church

endings.how: The book was spoiled by water or taken by thieves, and the merchant came and said so.
endings.text: Radger does not speak for a day. Then he asks for the covers. The bishop's letters go by another ship for three years.
endings.reward: flag bk_lost; the truth told is remembered: Radger will still teach letters to one of the crew

endings.how: The merchant sold the book in a heathen market for the gold on its boards.
endings.text: The price is the best of the year. It is known at York by Michaelmas and at Traiectum by Martinmas, and the gate is shut to the house for a generation.
endings.reward: silver, about a book's worth and half again; flag bk_lost; the church's standing lost here and at Dorestad

stories.reward: A standing order from the scriptorium, the bishop's surety, and a teacher of letters for the crew

stories.title: Bread until harvest
stories.summary: The king has ordered his bishops to feed the starving until harvest, and the prior's store is sacks short. A cargo of grain sold fairly here is paid for in prayers, in a charter or in the church's own silver, and the church does not forget which.
stories.picture: The gate of the fort at first light: a line of thin people with bowls, the prior with a tally board, a boat's crew carrying sacks up from the bank.

beats.text: Hildeburg says the prior has been to ask the price of her malt. He has never done that before.
Hadda shows the store. There is bread for the house till Saint John's and the poor come to the gate every morning. He asks what grain costs at Dorestad, and waits.
Grain at Dorestad is dear and getting dearer. From 794 the king's price is cried at the toll: a measure of rye for three pennies, of wheat for four, and no more.
The bishop offers three payments and lets the merchant choose: prayers by name at Saint Martin's, a charter, or silver from the altar plate at the king's price.
On the Almere shore the priest holds the bishop's measure while the grain is sold, and writes to Traiectum who sold fair.

endings.how: The grain was sold at or under the king's price.
endings.text: The gate opens every morning until harvest. The house's name is read at Saint Martin's on the bishop's own feast, and the prior stops checking the weight twice.
endings.reward: flag hy_fed_poor; deed fair_dealing; a charter to land free on the church's plots, or silver at the king's price

endings.how: The grain was given, for prayers only.
endings.text: Hamacar says nothing for a moment and then asks the merchant's father's name, to have it written with his own.
endings.reward: flag hy_fed_poor; deed gave_alms; the bishop's surety without further asking (flag db_surety)

endings.how: The merchant held out for the hungry price, here or up the river.
endings.text: The church pays and writes it down. The count's men ask about it at Dorestad before the year is out.
endings.reward: silver, half again above the king's price; flag hy_sold_dear

stories.reward: The church's lasting good word, a landing charter or the bishop's surety

stories.title: A boat for the priest
stories.summary: In 793 the churches east of the Lauwers burn and a priest comes over the Almere with nothing but a book. In 794 Liudger is back among the Frisians and asks his old school for a priest: the bishop has the man and no boat.
stories.picture: A small boat poling north up the Vecht among reeds at dawn, a young tonsured priest sitting very upright amidships with a wrapped bundle on his knees.

beats.text: A burned church, and a priest hiding in a byre who wants passage to Traiectum. Carrying him is noticed by both sides.
The priest sleeps two days. Hadda feeds him porridge and asks nothing. Hamacar asks everything, and writes to Liudger.
A young priest of the school is to go to the Ems mouth with a chalice, a book and a small bell. The way is the Vecht, the Almere and the coast, and he has never been in a boat.
On the Almere shore a Frisian asks, kindly, whether the priest would like to go home while he can. The priest asks what the man's children are called.
Liudger is there, leading his horse. Nobody is punished who comes to be shriven. The bell is hung from an oak branch until there is a roof.

endings.how: The priest was put ashore at the Ems mouth with his bell.
endings.text: Liudger blesses the boat by name. The Christians of the coast know the house; the wise woman knows it too, and is civil.
endings.reward: flag ms_carried_priest; deed carried_letters; a friend in cast.liudger; lodging at every church of the Frisian shore

endings.how: The merchant took the Frisian's advice and brought the priest home.
endings.text: The priest goes again by land with a pack horse and arrives at Christmas. Hamacar thanks the merchant for his caution, and sends his letters by another boat that year.
endings.reward: no silver lost; the old believers of the Almere shore think well of the house

endings.how: The priest was landed short, at the first safe beach.
endings.text: He walks the rest. He does not complain of it, which is worse, because Liudger asks.
endings.reward: the fare, paid in advance; the bishop's standing cooled

stories.reward: A friend in Liudger and the churches of the Frisian coast

stories.title: The chest goes inland
stories.summary: The fleet of 834 passes under the wall. In 857 it stops, and the bishop goes up the river for what turns out to be a lifetime. What a merchant carries out for the church that year, his grandchildren can bring home.
stories.picture: Night on the strand, the fort burning behind: canons handing a long iron-bound chest down into a small boat, an old priest with a staff standing in the water to his knees.

beats.text: Sails on the river, counted from the wall. They go by to Dorestad and do not stop. Odulf asks every skipper he knows for one promise.
Rorik's toll man says his lord has sailed for Denmark to try for a kingdom, and that he himself would move his goods upriver this summer.
The Danes come while Rorik is away. Bishop Hunger is leaving. The chest of books and the altar things of Saint Martin's are on the bank, and there are more chests than boats.
The clergy are given a church far up the Maas and later sit at Daventre. The chest is received, counted, and the house's name written on the inside of the lid.
Balderik is home and reads the lid. He sends for the heirs of the name he finds there.
The bishop's toll man on the Vecht side has the house on his board among the saint's own. He counts the hull all the same, for the pleasure of it.

endings.how: The house's boat took the chest up the river and left its own goods on the bank.
endings.text: The goods burn. Sixty years on, a bishop gives the heirs ground on the Stathe without rent and a place inside the wall in any alarm.
endings.reward: flags bk_carried and traiectum_chest_saved; from 920 the unlock traiectum.stathe_ground

endings.how: The chest was buried in the old graves west of the fort and the boat saved her own cargo.
endings.text: The books lie in the ground two winters before anyone dares fetch them, and the damp has been at them. The church is grateful, with reservations.
endings.reward: the cargo kept; half the standing of the other way; a fetch errand in 859 (open_fetch)

endings.how: The merchant had word in time and was gone before the sails came.
endings.text: Nobody blames a man for living. Nobody writes his name inside a lid either.
endings.reward: boat, crew and cargo whole; flag df_moved if the house then settles up the river

stories.reward: Rent-free ground on the Stathe for the heirs, and refuge inside the wall

stories.title: Our own fire
stories.summary: A year after Tiel burns, the same sails are on the Lek. The merchants of the Stathe do the Northmen's work for them and carry what they can into the bishop's fort.
stories.picture: The waterfront in flames from end to end in broad daylight, merchants with torches and bundles running for a bridge and a gate; far down the river, small and unhurried, a line of striped sails.

beats.text: Bernbod's cousin from Tiel arrives with a scale, a wife and nothing else, and tells it at every table.
Word on the Waal: the fleet is back and has turned north. A boat that leaves now reaches Traiectum half a day ahead of it.
The merchants meet in the street. Nothing left outside the wall, they say, and nothing for the Northmen to sit in. Bernbod picks up the first torch and looks round for the second.
From the wall: the fleet lies off the smoking bank a day, talks, and goes. No attack follows. Then everybody looks at what they have done.

endings.how: The merchant fired his own store with the rest and carried for his neighbours.
endings.text: The Stathe is built again by Martinmas, closer under the wall, and the house's berth is marked out first.
endings.reward: the store lost; a fast friend in traiectum.bernbod; a berth on the Vecht side for good (unlock traiectum.berth)

endings.how: The merchant loaded his goods and took the boat up the Vecht while the others burned.
endings.text: The goods are safe. The berth is not where he left it when he comes back, and nobody remembers moving it.
endings.reward: cargo whole; traiectum.bernbod cool for years

endings.how: The merchant went out in a small boat to talk to the Northmen in their own tongue.
endings.text: They ask what there is to take. He tells them the truth: ash and a wall. They laugh, trade him a little silver for his bread, and go.
endings.reward: silver for provisions; a name on the Stathe that is half praise and half suspicion; news of where the fleet goes next

stories.reward: A lasting berth and a friend on the Stathe, or a whole cargo and a cold welcome

stories.title: The schoolmaster's key
stories.summary: The Latin riddles go the monks' way, from school to school, and on the lower Rhine the way begins at Saint Martin's. Radger sets every new boy three lines about a key; a shipman who answers them is shown the chest of Liudger's books and sent on up the river to the next man with a riddle and nobody to try it on.
stories.picture: A schoolroom against a Roman wall: a stooped master holding up a small iron key between finger and thumb before a great chest, a row of boys on a bench craning to see, and a boatman in the doorway with his cap in his hand.

beats.text: Radger says his three lines: great strength out of a small body; it opens what is shut and shuts what is open; it keeps the house for its master, and he keeps it. It needs Latin only to read it; he says it aloud for a shipman. (riddle_symphosius_04_clavis.)
A merchant's son home from this school sets a riddle over Aldswith's ale about two iron points joined in one, and says who taught it him. (riddle_symphosius_61_ancora.)

The key answered, the chest is opened: the books Liudger carried home from York in a merchant's hull. Radger gives a leaf to copy, a riddle about the chest itself, and says what such a chest is worth and to whom. (aldhelm_89_arca_libraria; sets bk_knows_worth.)

Radger's friend the palace clerk has the next one on a wax tablet: the loud house and its silent guest. They send each other riddles by any boat that passes between the two houses, and yours is the boat. (riddle_symphosius_12_flumen.)
The moneyer's clerk at Dorestad was a boy on Radger's bench. He sells three lines about what money was before it was money, and asks after the old man's cough. (riddle_symphosius_91_pecunia.)

endings.how: You answered the key, the river and the money, and carried the answers back.
endings.text: Radger says you would have made a middling scholar, which from him is praise. The school's chest is open to your house, and boys who learned their letters there greet your boat in six ports for forty years.
endings.reward: Readings from the school's chest (the unlock traiectum.book_chest); standing with every church of the diocese; a step on the riddle road toward the harder sets.

endings.how: You carried the tablets between the two houses and never answered one.
endings.text: The schoolmaster and the clerk go on with their game through you, and pay for the carrying in wax and small favours. Neither of them ever asks what you thought the answers were.
endings.reward: Small freights and a friendly word at the school and the palace; no riddle reward.

endings.how: You sold the clerk's tablet to a schoolmaster further up the Rhine.
endings.text: It fetches eight pennies at Colonia, where they have it already. Radger hears of it within the year, as he hears of everything written on wax between here and Mogontia.
endings.reward: 8 d; the schoolmaster cool for as long as he lives.

stories.reward: A door into the schools of the Rhine, and the first Latin riddles of the road.

stories.title: The bishop's word
stories.summary: The count and the bishop share the district and dispute every fine in it. A house that has carried for Saint Martin's and sold it wax at a true weight can have the bishop stand surety on the Wōkerer's day; and when Dorestad is gone, it is to the bishop, here or in his exile at Daventre, that the house's reckoning is owed.
stories.picture: A formal bishop standing before his chair with one hand raised, a deacon writing at a sloping board, and between them on the table one half of a notched tally stick lying on a folded letter with a seal.

beats.text: Hadda the prior says what the bishop's good word costs: wax at a true weight, grain at a price the house can pay, and a book carried dry. He has seen four bishops, and it was the same with all of them.

beats.when: year < 807 and debt > 0 and not flag.db_surety
beats.text: Hamacar says before his deacon that Saint Martin's stands for this house on the Wōkerer's day. It is written down. He asks nothing for it, and the prior names nothing afterwards. (Sets db_surety.)
Hartwin the steward hears who stands for you, and counts your tally again. The count and the bishop dispute every fine; now they have you to dispute as well.
Liudger, whose priest you landed, offers a word to the bishop on your house's behalf. From him it weighs with Hamacar more than wax.

Dorestad is gone, and its count's day with it. The house's reckoning is owed to Saint Martin's now, and the bishop is not at home: his steward keeps the stick here, and the bishop keeps the answer at Daventre.

In the bishop's house by Lebuin's church the debt is reckoned in the church's way: so much silver, so much wax, so many letters carried. A house whose name is on the lid of a certain chest is given time.

endings.how: You earned the bishop's word and used it on the Wōkerer's day.
endings.text: The count gives the delay with a bad grace and remembers whose man you have made yourself. Saint Martin's expects its wax every Candlemas after, at a true weight, for as long as your house sails.
endings.reward: The spine's flag db_surety; the unlock traiectum.surety; a standing order for wax; the count a little colder.

endings.how: You sold to the church fairly and never asked it for anything.
endings.text: Hamacar notes it. His successors read the note. When the reckoning day moves to Traiectum two generations on, your house is the one that is asked what it can pay, not told.
endings.reward: The unlock traiectum.reckoning_day on easy terms for an heir; the prior's lasting good word.

endings.how: You took the bishop's surety and then let the day pass unpaid.
endings.text: Saint Martin's pays the count and holds your stick. A bishop does not seize a boat; he sends a clerk each Michaelmas who counts your cargo and sighs. It goes on for years.
endings.reward: The debt carried over to the church, with no interest and no forgetting; every priest in the diocese knows it.

stories.reward: A second lord for the house, slower than the count and harder to be rid of: surety now, and somewhere to reckon when Dorestad is gone.

works.name: A plot under the wall
works.what: A strip of the bishop's bank above the weed line, with a post-built shed and rollers of your own. It is held of the church for a yearly cake of wax.
works.needs: The prior's good word: wax or grain sold to the store at a fair weight at least twice.
works.gives: Goods may be left here between voyages; the boat lies above the flood; porters cost nothing.
works.picture: A new thatched shed on posts beside a boat on rollers, the pale wall of the fort close behind, a monk pacing out the boundary with a rope.
works.source: The church's own plots where its men land free (Design/content/realms/frisia_lotharingia.md); Carolingian occupation on the strand, 750-850 (De Bruijn, 'De vicus Stathe'). The rent in wax is a guess

works.name: A lamp before the altar
works.what: Oil and wax to keep one lamp burning before the altar of Saint Martin's for a year, with the giver's name said at Mass on Willibrord's day.
works.needs: Nothing but the silver, or three jars of oil in place of it.
works.gives: Standing with the bishop and the church's people on the river; the house is prayed for by name, which the crew like.
works.picture: A single hanging lamp of bronze over a small stone altar, a deacon on a stool trimming the wick, the rest of the church in the dark.
works.source: Oil for the lamps and chrism of the churches, scarce in the north (goods_793.json olive_oil); Willibrord's feast, 7 November (en.wikipedia 'Willibrord'). The custom here is likely, not attested

works.name: Stone for Balderik's gate
works.what: Boat loads of tuff from the Roman ruin at Vechten and lime from up the Rhine, for the gates and bastions the bishop is building.
works.needs: A boat that can carry stone, and the bishop's leave to take it from Vechten.
works.gives: A place for the house inside the wall in any alarm; the bishop's toll forgiven for ten years once he has one.
works.picture: A gateway half built in scaffolding of lashed poles, masons setting grey blocks, a barge of stone below on the river.
works.source: Balderik is said to have repaired the fort about 920 with gates, bastions and a west bridge (De Bruijn, 'De burcht Trecht'); Vechten robbed for the churches' stone (nl.wikipedia 'Fectio')

works.name: A berth on the Vecht side
works.what: Forty feet of the bank faced with oak posts and wattle, back-filled, with a storehouse whose door opens on the water.
works.needs: Ground on the Stathe, bought or given, and oak: old boat planks will do for the facing.
works.gives: A laden barge can lie alongside and load in a day; goods stored here are sold for you while you are away.
works.picture: Men driving oak posts into a river bank with a great wooden maul, wattle panels stacked ready, a new timber storehouse behind.
works.source: The Waterstraat dig, 1974-81: 420 m of revetments with timber houses and reused ship planks, 10th to 12th century (Research/traiectum_c800_notes.md; Design/content/ships.md)

works.name: A share in the merchants' church
works.what: The traders of the Stathe are building a church of their own outside the fort, so that they need not ask at the gate to hear Mass.
works.needs: A house or a berth on the Stathe, and Bernbod or his heirs speaking for you.
works.gives: A voice when the merchants meet; your dead are buried there; your oath is taken on the Stathe without witnesses from outside.
works.picture: A small church of timber and tuff going up among shop gables, merchants in good cloaks handing up beams themselves.
works.source: nl.wikipedia 'Buurkerk': the merchants' church, 10th or early 11th century. The merchants' rights are drawn from Tiel about 1020 (Alpertus II.20) and are a guess for Utrecht (?)

ships.how: built to order over a winter
ships.note: The boat of this river: one long Rhineland oak hollowed thin, spread with fire and water and raised with a plank a side. Aldlef and his like build one every second winter, if you bring the oak.
ships.picture: A half-hollowed oak trunk on trestles by the Vecht mouth, a man with an adze inside it up to his knees in chips.
ships.source: Vleuten 1, felled after about 734, about 15 by 1.10 m; Utrecht 1, 17.8 by 3.8 m, 997-1027 (Design/content/ships.md; nl.wikipedia 'Utrechtse schip')

ships.note: Fishers' and eel-trappers' dugouts lie all along the levee and change hands for a few pennies.
ships.picture: A narrow dugout nosed into the reeds with a fish trap of withies lying in it.
ships.source: Design/content/ships.md (logboats on the lower Rhine); a guess for this bank

ships.note: The church's errand boats and the ferry's old punts: sold when they leak more than they carry.
ships.picture: A flat punt on a pole crossing brown water, a monk and two sacks aboard.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json skiff_punt; the crossing gives the place its name

ships.note: The bishop's own river ship, lent with her crew to a house that carries his letters and his people; not for sale at any price.
ships.picture: A long low river ship with a striped awning aft and eight oars, a cross on a pole at the bow, lying under the fort wall.
ships.source: Bishops lent such ships: Hadebald of Cologne's two-cabin ship lent to Anskar in 826 (Rimbert, Vita Anskarii 7, Robinson 1921). That Utrecht's bishop had one is likely, not attested

ships.how: built to order over a winter
ships.note: Flat-bottomed barges of Ardennes oak for grain, wine and stone, built and broken up on the Vecht side.
ships.picture: A long flat barge with a short towing mast lying against a wattle-faced bank, casks being rolled aboard.
ships.source: Utrecht 3, after about 1004, 23 by 3.3 to 4 m, Ardennes oak (Design/content/ships.md)

ships.note: Sea-going ships come up to the Stathe now and are sometimes sold by a widow or a debtor. None is built here: the wrights of this river hollow oaks.
ships.picture: A round-bellied sailing ship with her yard lowered, moored among barges, a chalked mark of sale on her stem.
ships.source: Fragments of a keel ship reused in the Vecht quay, early 11th century (Design/content/ships.md, Utrecht 4); a second-hand sale is a guess (?)

sayings.text: 'Vaccipotens praesul': a bishop mighty in cows. (Alcuin's greeting to the bishop of Utrecht, still repeated at the guest table.)
sayings.source: Alcuin, carmen 4 (MGH Poetae I, 220-3), by 782; the Latin words only

sayings.text: 'Utpute non oleum nec vinum Fresia fundit.' Frisia gives no oil and no wine; so you will have honey, porridge and butter.
sayings.source: Alcuin, carmen 4; the Latin words, with our own paraphrase

sayings.text: 'Pando domos clausas, iterum sed claudo patentes.' I open shut houses and shut open ones. (The schoolmaster's riddle; the answer hangs round his neck.)
'Ec forsacho allum dioboles uuercum and uuordum, Thunaer ende Uoden ende Saxnote.' What a grown man is made to say at the font, east of here.
sayings.source: The Old Saxon baptismal vow, 776-800, perhaps from the Utrecht mission (texts_793.json saxon_vow)

sayings.text: The chest is full of holy words and knows none of them.
sayings.source: turned from Aldhelm, riddle 89, Arca libraria (texts_793.json aldhelm_89_arca_libraria); our own paraphrase

sayings.text: A Frank at the guest table, of the boatmen's short cloaks: 'What use is a napkin? In bed it does not cover me, on a horse it keeps off neither wind nor rain.'
sayings.source: Notker, Gesta Karoli I.34 (Grant 1907), paraphrased: Charlemagne on the short Frisian cloaks sold at the old price (?)

sayings.text: After Martin's goose, forty days of fish.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; Martinmas and the fast to Christmas: en.wikipedia 'Martin of Tours'

sayings.text: The Rhine goes to the sea. The Vecht goes home.
A margin in the school's psalter: 'The ink is thin, the day is short, and the prior says the tallow is counted.'
sayings.source: invented in the manner of scribes' marginal complaints

sayings.text: A church without a wall is a gift to the heathen.
sayings.source: invented; Balderik rebuilt the walls about 920 (De Bruijn, 'De burcht Trecht')

easter_eggs.text: The school's chest holds the books Liudger carried home from York, and a leaf inside the lid gives the year: 772, when the Angles and the Frisians fell out there and he left for his own safety.
easter_eggs.source: en.wikipedia 'Ludger'; Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I.11-12 (?). The leaf is invented

easter_eggs.text: An old book of Livy in the chest has a note in an 8th-century hand: 'Theutbert, bishop of Dorestad'. Radger cannot say who he was.
easter_eggs.source: Vienna, Cod. Lat. 15: a Livy with the owner's note; en.wikipedia 'Theodard of Utrecht'. That the book lay here in 793 is a guess (?)

easter_eggs.text: The bell of Saint Martin's is the one that rang with no hand on it in 754, when the count tried to keep Boniface's body here. The porter will show the rope and say it has been quiet since.
Ask Hadda about the poem. He knows by heart the lines in which he serves the porridge, and has never been told what the rest of it says about Dorestad's black-haired merchant.
easter_eggs.source: Alcuin, carmen 4: 'fugiens Dorstada relinque', 'niger Hrotberct', 'mercator avarus'

easter_eggs.text: West and east of the fort the plough turns up graves older than any church here: the dead of the Roman garrison's last years. The canons bury their own beside them and do not ask.
easter_eggs.source: De Bruijn, 'De burcht Trecht': early 5th-century graves west and east of the fort

easter_eggs.text: A day's poling up the river the burnt Roman fort of Vechten stands in the reeds. Every straight grey block in Traiectum's churches came out of it.

Liudger's mother was to be drowned at birth by her heathen grandmother's order. A neighbour put honey in the child's mouth, and a child that has eaten may not be killed. The guest table's honey is served with that story.
easter_eggs.source: Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I.6-7 (?): Liafburg; not checked in Altfrid's words

easter_eggs.text: Bishop Radboud, who never lived here, wrote a poem on a swallow. Bishop Adelbold wrote to a pope about the volume of a sphere. Both are copied in the school after 1010.
easter_eggs.source: nl.wikipedia 'Radboud van Utrecht', 'Adelbold II' (the letter to Gerbert)

easter_eggs.text: From Pentecost 1039 a stone in the cathedral choir is cut with the word 'exta'. The emperor is buried at Speyer. This part of him stayed.
In the posts of the Vecht quay are planks from a ship built the northern way, with iron rivets. Nobody on the Stathe will say whose she was.
easter_eggs.source: Design/content/ships.md: Utrecht 4, a Norse-built keel ship of the early 11th century, reused in the quay

easter_eggs.text: After 1034 a merchant in London may be offered the bones of Saint Odulf, stolen by raiders from Stavoren. An English bishop buys them for Evesham. Anyone who knew the old canon here will know the name.
easter_eggs.source: nl.wikipedia 'Odulfus': Bishop Aelfweard bought the relics in London

unlocks.what: the cathedral schoolmaster's riddle of the key
unlocks.how: Speak with Radger at the school, in any year from 793; Latin aboard, or a monk to read it out.

unlocks.what: a reading from the school's chest
unlocks.how: Solve the key riddle, or bring the school a book or parchment.
unlocks.gives: give_text aldhelm_89_arca_libraria; the easter egg of Liudger's books; flag bk_knows_worth

unlocks.what: a standing order from the scriptorium for calfskin, ink and wax tablets
unlocks.how: Carry a book or the bishop's letters safely (flag bk_carried) and come back to the school before 858.
unlocks.gives: flag bk_parchment; a yearly commission for parchment, pigments and wax at a fair fixed price

unlocks.what: the bishop stands surety for the house on the Wōkerer's day
unlocks.how: Carry the bishop's letters once and sell wax to the prior's store at a fair weight twice; ask at the hall.

unlocks.what: a charter to land free on the church of Utrecht's own plots
unlocks.how: Sell grain at or under the king's price in a hungry year (flag hy_fed_poor) and choose the charter.
unlocks.gives: no toll on goods landed on the church's plots at Dorestad, and later at Tiel and Daventre (toll)

unlocks.what: the house's reckoning day moves here
unlocks.how: After Dorestad is gone (863), settle at Traiectum or at Daventre and pay the year's debt before the bishop's steward.
unlocks.gives: flag df_moved; the Wōkerer's day is kept here

unlocks.how: An ancestor carried the church's chest inland in 857 (flag traiectum_chest_saved); speak with Balderik after 920.
unlocks.gives: the work traiectum.work.berth at half its cost; refuge inside the wall

unlocks.what: a berth on the Vecht side that nobody will dispute
unlocks.how: Burn your own store with the merchants in 1007 and help them carry.
unlocks.gives: a free berth and store; traiectum.bernbod a fast friend

unlocks.what: the Vecht learned: no pilot needed to the Almere
unlocks.how: Hire Aldlef as pilot three times, or be on friendly terms with him.
unlocks.gives: learn the Vecht channel; word sent ahead to Medemelacha

unlocks.what: Ground on the Stathe without rent, by Bishop Balderik's word
unlocks.how: An ancestor carried the church's chest inland in 857 (flag traiectum_chest_saved); ask Balderik what a name inside a lid is worth, between 920 and 975 (the card harbour.name_inside_the_lid.traiectum).
unlocks.gives: flag unlock_plot_traiectum: the unlock traiectum.stathe_ground in the engine's own flag; the bishop's toll man on the Vecht side counts the house among the saint's own (toll none)
